newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: West awaits signs of leadership change in N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: West awaits signs of leadership change in N.Korea.

text.p: North Korea next week marks the end of the traditional three-year mourning period for the late "Great Leader" Kim Il-sung, which political analysts say will clear the way for his son to formally assume national leadership.
But North Korea watchers said on Thursday there had been no signs so far that the Stalinist state was preparing any succession ceremony for Kim Jong-il, 55.
Although the junior Kim has been in full control of the North, the world may have to wait for months before witnessing communism's first dynastic succession, they said.

Jeong Se-hyun, head of the state-funded Research Institute for National Security in Seoul, said the North's constitution requires the ruling Workers' Party to call a central committee meeting three months before it elects its general secretary.
The party post and the state presidency have been left vacant since Kim Il-sung died on July 8, 1994.
"Kim Jong-il has been groomed as the political heir of his father since the 1980s. There's no reason Pyongyang has to hurry," Jeong said.
He said the North would also have to convene the Supreme People's Assembly to elevate him to state president.

"Unpredictable North Korea could ignore legal procedures, but lacking his father's charisma, Kim Jong-il would seek a proper wedding ceremony rather than live together with a girl and declare his marriage," Jeong said.

Lee Ho, South Korea's deputy unification minister in charge of analysing North Korean affairs, told Reuters that Kim Jong-il had successfully consolidated his power in the past three years by tightening his grip on the military.
As the supreme commander of the 1.1 million-strong army, the junior Kim has used the military for his public appearances. In April, he promoted 120 young loyal officers to generals.

Lee dismissed arguments that Kim Jong-il had scored diplomatic coups by opening a dialogue with the United States, agreeing to four-nation peace talks and clinching a landmark 1994 nuclear deal with Washington.
"The North's dire problems forced North Korea to accept compromises with the West. This underscores his failure to feed its citizens and stop the economy from crumbling," he said.

Famine-threatened North Korea formally agreed on Monday to a meeting on August 5 in New York of senior officials from the two Koreas, the United States and China to arrange four-nation talks on a peace treaty for the Korean peninsula.
It had previously insisted that any peace arrangement on the peninsula must be made directly by Washington and Pyongyang, excluding "U.S. puppet" South Korea.
"The North was recognising the fact that the South is the biggest potential investor and the biggest potential donor for food and other kinds of aid," a Western diplomat said.
Lee said North Korea, which was hit by devastating floods in 1995 and 1996, suffers from a chronic food shortage of two million tonnes annually even without a major natural disaster.
"Another large-scale flood could delay Kim Jong-il's succession," he added.
Analysts said clues on a leadership reshuffle could emerge when Pyongyang commemorates the third anniversary of Kim Il-sung's death next Tuesday.
"North Korea releases its hierarchy list during important events," said Cho Yong-ha, chief researcher at the independent Institute of North Korea studies.

"What is important to note is whether there will be major rises among the civilian elite. This will herald reshuffles in the cabinet and the party, which will probably be announced around the time Kim Jong-il is formally anointed," he said.
